Q3 GDP revision shows the economy was even stronger coming into the fourth quarter than previously thought.

Q3 GDP revised up well more than expected to 4.3% (est 3.5%; advance 3.4%), the fastest pace since Q3 2023. The 0.9-point upgrade was the biggest advance-to-second-estimate revision since Q2 2020, and since Q2 2015 excluding the pandemic.

▪️ Investment drove about half of the upgrade, led by software. Software spending grew 22.3% instead of 9.6% after BEA revised software prices to a 7.0% annualized decline from a 1.6% rise.
▪️ Information processing equipment added 0.95 point to growth, a record in data back to 1947.
▪️ Consumer spending was revised up to 4.2% (est 3.9%; advance 3.8%), the fastest since Q4 2024. Goods were revised up (pharmaceuticals, software, gasoline) and services down, with health care growth cut to 1.3% from 4.9%.
▪️ Final sales to private domestic purchasers were revised up to 5.8%, the most since Q2 2021.
▪️ Trade was still a big drag, with net exports subtracting 3.2 points, the most since Q1 2025.
▪️ The GDP price index was revised down to 1.9% (est 2.3%). PCE prices (2.1%) and core PCE (2.5%, in line) were unrevised.
▪️ Real GDI rose 4.4%, slightly faster than GDP, and the average of the two was also 4.4%, the most since Q4 2023.
▪️ Corporate profits rose $206B to a record $4.92T, up 21.3% from a year ago and a record 14.9% of GDP in data back to 1947. Nonfinancial profit margins were the highest since 1955.
▪️ The saving rate was revised down to 3.9%, the lowest since Q3 2022.

The US goods trade deficit jumped to $149.5B in October, driven by AI imports, far wider than the $135.6B expected and up from a revised $135.1B. That's the widest since March 2025, the third-widest on record and the 4th straight increase. 2026's deficit has now overtaken 2025's record pace.

▪️ Imports +6.1% to a record $365.3B, the biggest jump since January 2025, with all six major categories rising.
▪️ Capital goods imports (computers, chips and telecom gear for the AI buildout) +$13.4B to a record $171.4B, +80.0% from a year ago and up in 11 of the last 12 months.
▪️ That's the fastest growth on record: Q3 capital goods imports were up 59.8% year-over-year, topping the 56.4% of Q4 1972 in data back to 1967.
▪️ The capital goods deficit widened to $95.6B from $36.6B a year ago and accounted for about three-quarters of October's widening.
▪️ Exports were still up 3.2% to $215.8B, the most since April, including a record $75.8B in capital goods, but covered only about a third of the import jump.
▪️ Unlike the March 2025 tariff rush, when consumer goods led ($101.6B vs. $93.1B for capital goods) and the surge reversed within a month, now capital goods dwarf consumer goods ($171.4B vs. $61.4B), and the climb has been steady for more than a year.
▪️ The year-to-date deficit is about $1.070T, now above 2025's record pace ($1.047T). Topping 2025's full-year record would take only about $80B a month in November and December, and the monthly deficit hasn't been that low since January.
▪️ Q4 GDP: October's gap was $20.8B above the Q3 monthly average, pointing to another drag from trade, partly offset by inventory builds (wholesale +0.9%, retail +0.8%, both the most since July).
▪️ Not inflation-adjusted, and AI hardware import prices have been rising, so the full report on December 8 will show how much of the jump is real volume.

Source: Census Bureau, BEA, Bloomberg.

@C_Barraud's Morning Brief flags what may be the first sign China is going big to stop its stock slide. In a rare midday statement, the State Council pledged a bigger role for the "national team" of state buyers, with a liquidity pledge behind it. Per Bloomberg, it's the first recent State Council readout to name the national team. The CSI 300 jumped 4.2%, its best day since October 2024.

That matters because, as I noted in a post earlier this month, half-measures haven't worked, and the record since 2023 backs that up:

▪️ Beijing took 11 half-steps from July 2023 to January 2025: pledges, a trading-tax cut, short-selling curbs, a reserve cut and more. After every one, Shanghai closed lower within six months, by 2% to 13%.
▪️ This month's November 3 tools and November 6 State Council pledge were both followed by new lows.
▪️ But three forceful moves each marked the low: Huijin's $43B+ of ETF buying in Q1 2024, September 2024's stock-focused stimulus, and April 2025's Huijin buying with a central bank backstop. Shanghai was up 25%, 41% and 32% a year later.

Friday's statement is the closest Beijing has come to April 2025's open-ended commitment. 

What to watch: whether Huijin's ETF buying visibly steps up, and whether a rate cut follows. If the money follows the words, that's how Chinese bottoms have been made since 2023. If not, it may be just another bounce.

Another of the interesting items in @C_Barraud's Thursday Morning Brief was ZeroHedge's look at two Goldman notes. Together they map who has sold, who's still selling, and (with some data crunching) what the month so far bodes for forward returns.

▪️ Goldman's Tony Pasquariello says hedge funds sold global tech at the fastest pace in at least a decade over the past six weeks. In his view that's "genuine capitulation from fast money."
▪️ But the machines aren't done. As of Wednesday, Goldman's Futures Strats team estimated systematic funds had sold about $70B of global stocks over the prior week, with about $100B more to go over the following week. In their base case that then turns into small repurchases in early December, with "more of a V-shape" if the market rallies.
▪️ ZeroHedge calls that a possible Santa rally setup, but warns a mechanical bounce isn't a bottom. Goldman's Lee Coppersmith has seen hedge funds capitulate, but not the broad investor washout that has historically produced the strongest rebounds.

The S&P is down 5.2% for November through Wednesday, on track for its worst November since 2008 (−7.5%). So I went back to 1928 and looked at the 16 Novembers where the S&P fell 4% or more.
▪️ December was about normal: a median gain of +1.2%, higher 69% of the time, versus +1.5% and 72% in all years.
▪️ And the Santa Claus rally (the last five trading days of December plus the first two of January) actually ran hotter than usual: a median of +4.0% versus +1.4% normally. Since 1950 it was +5.7%, and higher in six of seven years.

So far so good.  But... 
▪️ The bounce usually didn't last. From the end of November to the end of March, the median was −3.9%, and only 6 of 16 years were higher, versus +3.5% and 63% in all years. The median low close over those four months was 8.5% below where November ended.
▪️ 2000 and 2008 are in the list. Both had strong Santa rallies (+5.7% and +7.4%), and both were down 11–12% by the end of March. There are exceptions on the other side though too: 1974 and 1987 both gained 12–19% by March, and both came right around major lows.

So history fits both sides. The good news: The repurchase-driven December pop Goldman describes has usually shown up after a bad November. The bad news: ZeroHedge's point that the last seller hasn't sold is backed by what came after December more often than not.

The @DailyChartbook nightly email Wednesday included an interesting post on the Nasdaq-100's underperformance vs the S&P 500. 

The former's 6-month return fell 8.66 points behind the S&P 500's on November 24, and the gap widened to 9.25 points at Wednesday's close. Their table shows the Nasdaq-100 itself has tended to do well after these extremes, averaging +30.2% over the next 12 months.

I was curious whether that was equally bullish for both indices or if it means the gap closes.  Using their same rule since 1986:

▪️ The Nasdaq-100 beat the S&P 500 over the next 6 and 12 months after 11 of the 13 completed signals.

▪️ The median 12-month gap was +10 points in the Nasdaq's favor, about double the +5.1 points you'd get on any random day since 1986.

▪️ The catch-up wasn't immediate. The median edge after one month was +0.5 points, no better than normal; most of it came in months two through six.

▪️ In those 11 wins, most of the damage was already done by the signal date. The Nasdaq-100 never fell more than about 5% further behind the S&P before turning.

The two exceptions are important though. After August 2000, the Nasdaq-100 trailed the S&P by another 43 points over the next year as the dot-com bust played out. After March 2022, it lagged by 2 points, and the gap first widened by nearly 11% as the Fed began hiking. In both cases the tech slide turned into a full tech bear market.

Today has whiffs of both. Elsewhere in the same email, there were notes that chip shares have fallen faster than in 2000 and that the link between AI stocks and broader risk appetite is near a six-year high (Goldman Sachs).

History favors tech closing the gap from here, but it also says the line to watch is whether the Nasdaq-100 falls more than about 6% further behind the S&P from the November 24 signal.  In that case, it's tracking 2000 and 2022 rather than the usual rebound. So far, it has slipped about 0.4% further.

The day after Thanksgiving is usually one of the quietest sessions of the year for stocks, but before you decide to overindulge, note that’s not normally the case when the VIX is elevated heading in.

Since 1990, the S&P 500’s post-Thanksgiving session has normally been tame, with an average intraday range of 0.7%, vs. 1.2% for all days.

But when the VIX is above 20 heading in (14 years), that average range expands to 1.0%, and 8 of the 10 most volatile post-Thanksgiving sessions have come with the VIX over 20.

With the VIX at 25 or higher (6 years), it’s even more so: a 1.3% average range, with 5 of the 6 ranking among the 10 most volatile sessions.

Direction has been a literal coin flip: higher in 7 of the 14 high-VIX years.

Context: Wednesday’s VIX close of 28.3 was the 4th-highest heading into Thanksgiving since 1990 (behind 2008, 2011 and 1997).

Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos will be the next ECB president. Eurozone leaders backed him unanimously in Brussels on Thursday after the Netherlands dropped its own candidate, former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot, according to the FT. The formal sign-off is due in December, and he takes over when Christine Lagarde leaves on February 7, nine months before her term ends, and chairs his first policy meeting on March 18.

De Cos is a win for the moderates. Knot was the pick for those most worried about inflation and debt. De Cos is seen as more dovish on rates, per Bloomberg, though Reuters notes colleagues call him a pragmatic moderate who can't be boxed in as a dove, and he has a record of preaching fiscal discipline as Bank of Spain governor.

What he inherits:

▪️ Euro-area inflation at 4% in October, double the ECB's 2% target;
▪️ Two ECB rate hikes already this year (June and September), with swaps pricing a third, to 2.75%, at the December 17 meeting, per the FT, and only one more expected after that as oil prices retreat and inflation is set to ease from the spring, per Reuters;
▪️ France's 10-year yield hitting 5% last month for the first time since 2002, with France and Belgium both struggling to pass budgets.

De Cos was just one of several changes at the top. 

Laurence Boone takes over Isabel Schnabel's markets portfolio, the seat that runs the ECB's bond-buying tools. Markus Brunnermeier replaces Philip Lane as chief economist in June. So Germany will have no one on the Executive Board from January to June, right through France's budget fight and the first round of its presidential election in April.

The rate path into next year probably doesn't change much. Lagarde remains president until early February, and the Governing Council is in hiking mode. De Cos also said recently that central banks need to stay vigilant on inflation. 

The bigger shift may be the backstop. A consensus-builder as president, a French economist running market operations and no German on the board for five months point towards an ECB perhaps more willing to step in if French spreads blow out. 

Reuters makes the same point, noting that de Cos is an ally of Mario Draghi, the "whatever it takes" president. SocGen's Michala Marcussen told Bloomberg that for markets, the question is "what kind of direction the ECB toolkit will be taken in." So it may be that the French-German 10-year spread is the chart to watch into April.
